* tools: Add and configure PHPStan static analysis

* Upgrade to PHPStan 2 and phpstan-wordpress 2

Require PHPStan 2.1 or newer and phpstan-wordpress 2.0 or newer, which
brings in the matching WordPress stubs. Rename the Composer script from
`analyse` to `phpstan`, as in WordPress core, and give it the same
memory limit.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Scan the built PHP files for the generated functions

The `gutenberg_*` functions and `*_Gutenberg` classes that `lib/` calls
are generated into `build/` by the build, so scan that directory. This
lets the ignore rule for unknown `gutenberg_*` functions go, and
`packages/` no longer needs to be scanned.

Also bring the paths up to date: `post-content.php` no longer exists, the
`html-api` compat directories were removed when the minimum WordPress
version went to 6.7, and executing `gutenberg.php` at bootstrap is not
needed for discovery. In the bootstrap, `SITECOOKIEPATH` and
`WP_TEMPLATE_PART_AREA_UNCATEGORIZED` are no longer referenced, while
`MEDIA_TRASH` now is; it is listed as a dynamic constant so that its
placeholder value is not treated as certain.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Analyze at rule level 5 with a single baseline

Start at rule level 5, as WordPress core does, and replace the per-level
PHP baselines for levels 0 through 8 with a single standard
`tools/phpstan/baseline.neon`, generated with PHPStan's
`--generate-baseline`. Report unmatched ignored errors, so baseline
entries are removed as the errors they cover are fixed.

Drop the ignore rule for unknown `gutenberg_*` functions, which the
scanned build files now resolve, and the level 6 ignore rule for the
WPCS iterable syntax. Leave `treatPhpDocTypesAsCertain` at its default,
as core does.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Match WordPress core's PHPStan analysis settings

Set `phpVersion` to the supported range of PHP 7.4 through 8.5, so the
results do not depend on the PHP version PHPStan runs on, and store the
result cache in `.cache/phpstan` so CI can reuse it.

Also set `treatPhpDocTypesAsCertain` to false, as core's
`tests/phpstan/base.neon` does. This corrects the earlier commit that
claimed core leaves it at its default. PHPDoc types are not enforced by
PHP, so callers can pass values that do not match them.

With PHPDoc types no longer treated as certain, PHPStan can no longer
prove the always-false conditions in `gutenberg_tinycolor_bound01()` and
`gutenberg_tinycolor_hsl_to_rgb()`, and the ignore comments for them
became unmatched errors. They are turned into plain comments, which keep
the explanation of why the conditions never hold. The baseline is
regenerated.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Run PHPStan in the unit test workflow

Add a PHP static analysis job alongside the PHPCS job. It reuses the
`build-assets` artifact that the PHP unit test jobs already download,
since the build generates the PHP files defining the `gutenberg_*`
functions and `*_Gutenberg` classes that PHPStan scans, so the build does
not run twice. Errors are reported as annotations on the pull request.

The result cache is restored from the latest run for the same week,
configuration, and dependencies, and each run saves its own. The job is
added to the status check's `needs`, so its result counts.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Document running PHPStan in the coding guidelines

Explain how to run the analysis locally, why the build has to run first,
how to regenerate the baseline when a change fixes a baselined error, and
how to override the configuration with an ignored `phpstan.neon`.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Declare the PHP polyfills that WordPress provides

With `phpVersion` starting at PHP 7.4, PHPStan reported the newer PHP
functions that WordPress polyfills in `wp-includes/compat.php`, such as
`str_contains()` and `array_is_list()`, as not found. The WordPress stubs
omit them, since they are defined conditionally, and core avoids the
problem only because it analyzes `compat.php` itself. That added 95 false
`function.notFound` errors to the baseline.

Declare them in a scanned `tools/phpstan/polyfills.php`, with the
signatures of the native functions. Only the polyfills available in the
minimum supported WordPress version, 7.0, are declared, so relying on one
added in 7.1, such as `clamp()`, is still reported.

With `array_is_list()` known, PHPStan now also reports a redundant
`array() !== $current` check in `Gutenberg_View_Config_Data`, which core
already dropped in its copy. It is left in the regenerated baseline.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Analyze all the PHP that WordPress core ships from Gutenberg

Core copies the PHP in `block-library`, the widget blocks, `core-fields`,
and `core-actions` verbatim, and ships the PHP generated from the
`wp-build` templates, but excludes these copies from its own PHPStan
analysis because they are generated. The style engine and the default
block parser are synced into core as well. None of this was analyzed
anywhere, so analyze it here, where it is maintained.

The `wp-build` templates are not valid PHP, so the generated files in
`build/` are analyzed instead. The `node_modules` directories are
excluded from analysis and scanning, as in core, since the parser
package's dependencies include PHP.

The baseline is regenerated, now with 251 errors, of which 166 are in
the newly analyzed code: 145 in `block-library`, 16 from one line of
the page template, four in the style engine, and one in `core-actions`.
The docs say what the analysis covers.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Analyze the wp-build PHP templates themselves

The PHP files that the build generates from the wp-build templates were
analyzed in `build/`, so problems in the templates were found, but they
were reported against the generated files: once for each page generated
from the page template, and never on the template line to change.

Analyze the templates instead. They are not valid PHP until the build
replaces their `{{PLACEHOLDER}}` tokens, so `WpBuildTemplateParser`
wraps the parser that PHPStan uses for analyzed files and substitutes a
representative value for each token first, modeled on what the build
generates. No substitution spans more than one line, so every reported
error, including a syntax error, points at the template line itself,
locally and in the annotations in CI. An unknown placeholder is reported
as such, rather than as a syntax error.

The templates are listed one by one, from a PHP config include that
globs them, rather than as their directory. PHPStan finds the functions
declared in an analyzed directory by reading the raw files, which fails
on a template, whereas it finds those in an analyzed file by parsing it.

The class is autoloaded from `tools/phpstan/src`. The regenerated
baseline has 237 errors, with the 16 for the empty script source in the
generated pages now two, one for each page template.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Correct the version comment on the composer-install pins

The pinned commit of `ramsey/composer-install` is its `4.0.0` tag; the
action has no `v4.0.0` tag, so zizmor reports the comment as not matching
the pin. Correct it for all three jobs that use the action, as core's
workflows already write it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Ignore Zizmor's cache poisoning finding for the unit test workflow

Zizmor treats a workflow that runs on pushes to `release/*` branches as
one that publishes release artifacts, and reports every cache its jobs
restore as open to cache poisoning: an attacker who could write a cache
entry on trunk could have it restored into the release build. Without
that trigger, the same workflow has no findings, which is also why
core's workflows, which cache in the same way, have none.

Nothing built in this workflow is published, though. Its jobs only
report test and lint results, and the `build-assets` artifact is only
used by its own jobs. So ignore the finding, with a single comment on
the `push` trigger that causes it, which covers the new PHPStan job's
two caches as well as the three that the PHP test and PHPCS jobs
already had. The comment above it explains the reasoning, and that the
ignore should go if the workflow ever publishes what it builds.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Use a native property type and only PHPStan's public API in the template parser

Declare the wrapped parser property with a native `Parser` type, since
PHPStan requires PHP 7.4 or newer.

The parser also constructed `ParserErrorsException` and called its
`getErrors()`, neither of which is covered by PHPStan's backward
compatibility promise, so a minor PHPStan release could break them.
Neither is needed:

* A syntax error in a rendered template already gets reported against
  the template being analyzed, so it no longer has to be rethrown with
  the file name.
* An unreadable template is handed to the wrapped parser, which reports
  it as it does for any other file.
* A placeholder without a substitute is a gap in the parser rather than
  an error in the template, so it now throws a `LogicException` naming
  the placeholder, its line, and the template, which fails the run.

The parser now has no errors at rule level 10.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Address PhpStorm's inspections in the PHPStan tooling

* Rename the polyfill declarations to `polyfills.stub`, the extension
  PHPStan uses for files that only declare signatures. Their empty
  bodies are what a stub is, but as a `.php` file PhpStorm analyzed them
  as code and reported each one as missing a `return` statement.
* In the template parser, import `LogicException` and the `Stmt` node
  class rather than qualifying them, drop the redundant escapes of the
  closing braces in the placeholder pattern, and name the `parseString()`
  parameter `$sourceCode` as the interface does, so that it can be
  passed as a named argument.
* Declare the bootstrap constants with `const` rather than `define()`.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Add a phpstan:baselines Composer script, as in core

Regenerating the baseline meant spelling out
`composer phpstan -- --generate-baseline=tools/phpstan/baseline.neon`.
Add a `phpstan:baselines` script for it, named as in WordPress core so the
same command works in both. Core's script runs a wrapper that splits its
baselines by error identifier; Gutenberg keeps a single baseline, so its
script only passes PHPStan's own `--generate-baseline` the file to write.
It also passes `--allow-empty-baseline`, so the baseline can still be
regenerated once its last error is fixed.

The configuration comment and the coding guidelines now name the script.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Add typecheck:php npm scripts that run PHPStan in wp-env

Add `typecheck:php` and `typecheck:php:baselines`, named as in WordPress
core, which run the `phpstan` and `phpstan:baselines` Composer scripts.
Core runs them in its own Docker environment; here they run in the
`wp-env` CLI container, as `lint:php` does for PHPCS, so contributors
without a local PHP can run the analysis. Arguments after `--` are
passed on to PHPStan.

The bare `typecheck` script stays the TypeScript check, the way `lint`
does not include `lint:php`: it runs in CI and in the editor workflow
without the local environment, which these need.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* List the PHPStan errors in the job summary

An annotation is only shown alongside the changes in a pull request when
its line is part of the diff, and GitHub shows at most ten error
annotations per step. An error on a line the pull request did not
change, or one with no line at all, was otherwise only in the log, with
nothing but a failed check to show for it.

PHPStan now writes a JSON report, which `phpstan-report.js` turns into the
annotations, and into a job summary listing every error with a link to
its line. An out-of-date baseline, the most common error away from the
changed lines, gets its own explanation there: it is expected after a
pull request fixes a baselined error, and the fix is to regenerate the
baseline with `composer phpstan:baselines`, rather than to change the
code. The job still fails on any error.

This follows the report that core's PHPStan workflow writes, but keeps
the errors as errors rather than warnings, since Gutenberg merges on
GitHub and relies on its checks to keep new errors out.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Let a local PHPStan configuration opt in to analyzing the tests

The tests in `phpunit/` are not analyzed by default, since they do not
ship in core, but a local `phpstan.neon` can now add them to the paths:

* Require `phpstan/phpstan-phpunit`, the PHPUnit extension core uses,
  which the extension installer enables. It only acts on test code, so
  the regular analysis is unaffected.
* Require `php-stubs/wordpress-tests-stubs` and scan it, for the
  WordPress test library that wp-env only provides at runtime, such as
  `WP_UnitTestCase` and its factories. Without it, analyzing the tests
  reports 4,832 errors, nearly all for those unknown classes; with it,
  287.
* Define the constants the test bootstrap provides, `DIR_TESTDATA` and
  `WP_TESTS_DOMAIN`, and `WP_TEMPLATE_PART_AREA_UNCATEGORIZED`, which the
  WordPress stubs lack.

The last of those also resolves two `constant.notFound` errors in the
template part block, so they are removed from the baseline. The coding
guidelines show the configuration that opts in to the tests.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Always generate the baseline from phpstan.neon.dist

PHPStan uses `phpstan.neon` in place of `phpstan.neon.dist` when it
exists, so with a local configuration, such as one that raises the rule
level or adds the tests, `composer phpstan:baselines` would have written
that configuration's errors into the committed baseline. Pass
`phpstan.neon.dist` explicitly, as core's baseline generator does, so the
baseline only ever records what CI analyzes. The `typecheck:php:baselines`
npm script runs the same Composer script.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Explain why the PHPStan report script prints the annotations

The annotations were printed by PHPStan itself before, with its `github`
error format. Say in the script's docblock that it now prints them because
PHPStan writes JSON for the job summary, and can only produce one format
per run. Also correct the claim that errors away from the changed lines
were otherwise only in the log: they are listed with the run's
annotations, unless they fall past the tenth.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Revert an accidental change to gutenberg.php

The previous commit swept in a throwaway test change that was staged at
the time, renaming the `plugin_basename()` call to a function that does
not exist. Restore the line.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Pin the PHPStan packages to exact versions

There is no lock file, so a caret range installs whatever was released
last. A new PHPStan release, or new WordPress stubs, can report new
errors or stop reporting baselined ones, and with
`reportUnmatchedIgnoredErrors` either fails CI on every pull request at
once. Pin the versions the baseline was generated with, as core does, so
an upgrade is a deliberate change that regenerates the baseline.

The WordPress stubs were only required through the WordPress extension,
so require them directly to pin them as well. The extension installer
stays a range, since it does not affect the results.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Only advise regenerating the baseline when an error was fixed

PHPStan reports `ignore.count` both when a baselined error occurs fewer
times than recorded and when it occurs more times. The job summary
treated both as a stale baseline and advised regenerating it, which in
the second case would record a newly added occurrence as accepted.

Tell the two apart by PHPStan's message, which says "occurred only" when
there are fewer. Keep the advice to regenerate for that case, and for the
other say that the pull request likely added an occurrence to fix.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Leave the baseline out of the PHPStan cache key

The key hashed every file in `tools/phpstan`, including the baseline, so
each pull request that fixed a baselined error started from an empty
cache and saved a cache of its own under a new key. The baseline only
filters the reported errors, so leave it out, as core does.

The `tools/phpstan/*` pattern also did not match the parser in
`tools/phpstan/src`, which does change the analysis, so hash that too.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Report a PHPStan run that wrote no report

PHPStan also exits with 1 when it cannot load the configuration, and
then writes the reason to stderr and nothing to the report. The run step
lets that status through as a run with errors, and the report script then
failed on `JSON.parse` with a Node stack trace that did not say what went
wrong.

Say instead, as an annotation and in the job summary, that PHPStan did
not complete, and point to the run step's output for the reason.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* List at most 500 PHPStan errors in the job summary

GitHub drops a job summary larger than 1 MiB entirely, so a run with
thousands of errors, such as after a PHPStan upgrade, would have shown
none of them there. List the first 500 and say how many more are in the
step's output, where every error is still printed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Locate PHPStan errors in traits by the trait's file

PHPStan keys an error in a trait by the trait's file followed by
" (in context of class Foo)", for the class it was analyzed in. Passed
through as the path, the annotation did not attach to the file and the
link in the job summary led to a page that does not exist. Strip the
suffix.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Discover the functions the wp-build templates declare

PHPStan finds the symbols a file declares by parsing it with its simple
parser, not the rich parser used for the analysis, and only the rich
parser was replaced to render the templates. Parsing a raw template
failed, so none of its functions were found. The analysis still passed
because the templates were rendered with the `gutenberg` prefix, and the
scanned files in `build` declare functions by the same names. A call in
a template was therefore checked against the built function, which can
be out of date with the template.

Replace the simple parser as well, and render the templates with a
prefix that no built file uses, so that a template's calls resolve to
the template's own functions.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Pin the PHPStan extension installer too

It was left as a range since it only includes the configuration of the
extensions that are installed, which are pinned. A new release could
still change how it does that, though, and it costs nothing to pin, so
every package that affects the analysis is now at an exact version.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Analyze against the WordPress 7.0 stubs

The plugin supports WordPress 7.0, but the stubs were those of 7.1, which
declare the functions, classes, and methods added in 7.1. A call to one
of them without a guard would pass the analysis, and then be a fatal
error on 7.0. This also contradicts the polyfill stubs, which leave out
the 7.1 polyfills for this very reason.

Pin the stubs to 7.0.1, the latest release for 7.0, and regenerate the
baseline. Nothing it newly reports fails on 7.0:

* The calls to `register()` and `unregister()` on the result of
  `WP_Icons_Registry::get_instance()` reach the Gutenberg subclass, which
  replaces the shared instance when it loads, and in which both are
  public.
* The call to `WP_Theme_JSON::get_viewport_media_queries()` in the
  Navigation block is guarded by `method_exists()`.
* The rest are argument types that the 7.0 stubs declare differently.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* List PHPStan errors that belong to no file first

The errors that are not specific to a file, such as an internal error or
a configuration problem, were added after all the others, so the limits
of 10 annotations and 500 summary rows dropped them first. They are
about the run itself, and the hardest to find in the log, so put them
first instead.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Only advise regenerating the baseline when nothing else is reported

When a pull request changes a line with a baselined error, the error can
come back with a different message, so that its baseline entry no longer
matches and the error is reported as a new one. The job summary then
said that the baseline was out of date and should be regenerated, which
would record the new error as accepted.

When the run reports other errors alongside out-of-date entries, say to
fix those first, and only then regenerate the baseline.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Only save the PHPStan result cache on trunk

Every run saved a cache of its own. One saved for a pull request can only
be restored by that pull request, though, so with the number of pull
requests this repository gets, these would mostly use up its cache
storage and push out the caches that every run restores, such as those
for npm and Composer.

Restore the cache in every run, and save it only on pushes to trunk, so
that pull requests start from the latest cache of trunk.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Point from wp-build's template replacements to the PHPStan parser

The parser that renders the templates for PHPStan substitutes a sample
value for each placeholder, modeled on what the build generates. A
placeholder it does not know fails the analysis, but if what a known
placeholder expands to changes shape, the parser goes on analyzing the
old one without notice. Say where the sample values are, next to the
function that applies the real ones.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Analyze against stubs generated from WordPress core trunk

Gutenberg tracks core trunk, so the stubs released for a WordPress
version lack what trunk has added since, and the analysis would report
code that uses it. The 7.0 stubs it used instead report a call to a
trunk function as not found, and miss core's newer types.

Until php-stubs/wordpress-stubs publishes stubs built from trunk,
generate them with its generator from a pinned trunk commit, r64757,
which no longer has the global type aliases that the stubs could not
carry. The generator is pinned to the head of its PR 498, without which
it adds a second `@phpstan-return` to the docblocks that now have their
own in core.

The stubs are committed in tools/phpstan/wordpress-stubs/ as a path
package named php-stubs/wordpress-stubs, in place of the released one,
since szepeviktor/phpstan-wordpress loads them from that package's path.
The stubs have the .stub extension and are marked as generated in
.gitattributes, with a small PHP file at the expected path to load them.
They are also part of the CI cache key for the PHPStan result cache.

Regenerate the baseline, from which 18 entries go, while 2 calls that
only WordPress 7.0 or 7.1 need are now reported.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Explain the block passed to wp_get_elements_class_name()

Since WordPress 7.1 the function takes no parameters, and the trunk
stubs report the block passed to it. WordPress 7.0, which the plugin
still supports, requires the block, while 7.1 ignores it. Keep the
argument, and ignore the error inline with that reason in place of its
baseline entry.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Explain the guard for core's reaction summary pre-fetching

The trunk stubs declare WP_REST_Comments_Controller's
prefetch_reaction_summaries(), so the method_exists() guard that skips
Gutenberg's own pre-fetching is reported as always true. The method
does not exist before WordPress 7.2, so keep the guard, and ignore the
error inline with that reason in place of its baseline entry.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Declare the clamp() polyfill from WordPress 7.1

The polyfill stubs left out those added in WordPress 7.1, so that the
analysis matched the minimum supported version. Now that the WordPress
stubs follow core trunk, the polyfills follow it too.

Of the three that were omitted, only `clamp()` needs declaring, since
PHPStan already knows `mb_chr()` and `mb_ord()` as mbstring functions.
Also correct why the stubs omit compat.php: a polyfill there would
redeclare a native function when the stubs are executed as a bootstrap
file.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Mark the PHPStan stub files as PHP

Linguist does not recognize the .stub extension, so GitHub shows the
polyfill stubs and the generated WordPress stubs as plain text. Set
their language to PHP, and use Git's PHP diff driver so that the hunk
headers name the enclosing function.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Add a wp-build changelog entry for the template replacement note

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Run the WordPress stubs generator as a Composer script

The generator could only be found by looking in tools/phpstan. Expose
it as `composer phpstan:generate-wordpress-stubs`, next to the other
PHPStan scripts, and describe in the coding guidelines how to update
the stubs.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Note the SVN revision and version of the pinned core commit

A bare commit hash says nothing about how recent the stubs are. Follow
it with the SVN revision and the $wp_version at that commit, the way a
pinned GitHub action is followed by its version.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Say that generating the WordPress stubs is temporary

Once php-stubs/wordpress-stubs publishes builds from core trunk, a
pinned one can be required like any other dependency. Say so in the
generator, along with what to remove then.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Generate the WordPress stubs from trunk, a core PR, or a checkout

A Gutenberg change often depends on a wordpress-develop pull request
that adds what it uses, and with the stubs pinned to a trunk commit in
the script, the analysis reported those uses until the core change was
committed and the pin bumped by hand.

The generator now takes the source as an option: `--commit=<ref>`, such
as `trunk`, `--pr=<number>` for the head of a core pull request, or
`--checkout[=<path>]` for the working tree of a wordpress-develop
checkout, by default the one Gutenberg is in, with any uncommitted
changes to tracked files. A commit is read from that checkout when it
has it, and is fetched from GitHub otherwise.

The commit is no longer hard-coded in the script. The package's
composer.json records the source, so that running the generator with no
option reproduces the stubs, and the stub header says where they came
from: the trunk commit and its revision, or the pull request and the
trunk revision it is based on. Stubs generated from a pull request are
meant to be committed with the change that depends on it, and
regenerated from trunk once the core change is committed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Cache the stubs generator, and allow overriding its source

Each run fetched the generator and installed its dependencies again.
Keep it set up in .cache/wordpress-stubs-generator, by repository and
commit, and generate in a copy, so that the cached one stays unchanged.
With the wordpress-develop commit in the enclosing checkout too, a run
then needs no network at all.

The generator's repository and commit, the wordpress-develop
repository, and the cache directory can now be overridden with
environment variables, such as to try a generator change. The stub
header names the generator repository that was used.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Generate the WordPress stubs on demand instead of committing them

The stubs are a 6 MB generated file, which every pull request that
updates them carries as a diff. The package's composer.json already
records the core commit or pull request they are generated from, so
commit only that, and ignore the stubs.

Run with no option, the generator now does nothing when the stubs were
generated from that source, and generates them otherwise. The stubs
record a key for the source, the generator, and the script itself, so a
pull that changes any of them generates them again. Only the options
write the recorded source, so a regeneration leaves composer.json as it
